exercises.prompt: What does this C program print? (Give all three numbers, in order, separated by spaces.)
exercises.explanation: A `static` local variable is initialized once and keeps its value across calls, unlike an ordinary local which is recreated fresh every time. `id++` returns the old value then increments, so successive calls yield 100, 101, 102.

exercises.prompt: What does this C++ program print? (Give both numbers, in order, separated by a space.)
exercises.explanation: Since C++11, integer division truncates toward zero rather than flooring, so $-7/2 = -3.5$ truncates to $-3$ (not $-4$). The remainder then satisfies $(-3)\times 2 + r = -7$, so $r=-1$ — negative, matching the sign of the dividend, which surprises developers used to Python's floor-toward-negative-infinity `//`.

exercises.prompt: This function is meant to print 'Weekend' exactly once for day 6 (Saturday). What actually happens when `describe(6)` is called, and why?
choices: It prints 'Weekend' twice — the `case 6` branch has no `break`, so execution falls through into `case 7`
It prints 'Weekend' once, exactly as intended, since `day` only matches one case
It prints 'Weekday', because `default` always runs after any matched case
It's a compile error, since two cases can't print the same string
exercises.answer: It prints 'Weekend' twice — the `case 6` branch has no `break`, so execution falls through into `case 7`
exercises.explanation: C's `switch` falls through to the next case by default unless a `break` stops it. `case 6` has no `break`, so after printing once it continues straight into `case 7`'s `printf` too, printing 'Weekend' a second time before finally hitting `break`.

exercises.prompt: What is the time complexity of `dedupe` as a function of `n = len(items)`, in the worst case (e.g. when every item is already distinct)?
exercises.explanation: There's only one loop, but `x not in result` scans the entire `result` list built so far — which grows to length $n$ in the worst case. Summing $1+2+\dots+n$ gives $O(n^2)$ total work, a classic 'hidden' quadratic hiding inside code that looks linear at a glance.

exercises.prompt: For a non-negative integer `n`, what does `mystery(n)` compute?
choices: The number of 1 bits in n's binary representation
The position of the lowest set bit in n
n rounded down to the nearest power of 2
The number of trailing zero bits in n
exercises.answer: The number of 1 bits in n's binary representation
exercises.explanation: `n & (n - 1)` always clears exactly the lowest set bit of `n` (e.g. `0b1011 & 0b1010 = 0b1010`). The loop runs once per set bit until `n` reaches 0, so `count` ends up counting the 1 bits — this is Brian Kernighan's classic popcount trick.
